sorular.konu: Fine-Tuning Data Format and Instruction Tuning
sorular.soru: During pretraining, a base model learned from a huge amount of general text. Why do we still fine-tune it with task-specific examples?
secenekler: To learn general language patterns from books and web pages
To store its weights in fewer bits so that it fits on a small GPU
To teach it how to respond to the specific task we care about
To check how well it works on examples it has never seen
sorular.aciklama: Pretraining gives the model general language skills, and fine-tuning on task pairs teaches it how to respond to one task. Learning general patterns from books and web pages is the job of pretraining, and that step is already done.

sorular.soru: A hospital has a large set of unlabeled medical reports. It wants the model to become familiar with medical language. Which approach fits best?
secenekler: Continued pretraining, because it learns domain language from raw text
Supervised fine-tuning, because it learns domain language from raw text
Continued pretraining, because it teaches the model to answer requests
Supervised fine-tuning, because it works without any labels or answers
sorular.aciklama: Continued pretraining keeps predicting the next token on raw domain text, so the model gets used to the language of the field. Supervised fine-tuning needs instruction and gold answer pairs, and it teaches answer behavior rather than domain language.

sorular.soru: A team fine-tunes a model and checks its errors only on the training examples. What is the main problem with this plan?
secenekler: The gradients will be wrong, because they need held-out examples
The model will forget the skills it learned during pretraining
They will have to run the final test again after every update
They cannot see whether the model will work on new examples
sorular.aciklama: Errors on seen examples can be very low even when the model has only memorized them, so we need held-out validation data to judge real performance. The gradients come from the training loss, so they do not need held-out examples.

sorular.soru: During SFT, the model already gives the gold answer token a very high probability. What does this mean for the training step on this example?
secenekler: The loss is large, because the model is too sure about its answer
The loss is small, so there is little left to learn from this example
The loss moves to the prompt tokens, since the answer is already right
The loss is skipped, because the optimizer learns only from mistakes
sorular.aciklama: Cross-entropy looks at the probability of the gold token, so a high probability gives a small loss and only a small weight change. Training still uses the loss when the model is right, but its value is close to zero.

sorular.konu: Fine-Tuning Data Format and Instruction Tuning
sorular.soru: Before SFT, a user asks a base model to classify a review and answer with one word. Instead, it writes a long sentence that continues the text. Why?
secenekler: It has no classification head, so it cannot pick one of the labels
It reads text in both directions, so it cannot give a short answer
It learned to continue text, but not yet to follow an answer format
It stores its weights in fewer bits, so its output is less exact
sorular.aciklama: Pretraining teaches next-token prediction, so a base model tends to continue the text instead of following the request. An LLM does not need a classification head, because SFT teaches it to write the label itself as text.

sorular.konu: Fine-Tuning Data Format and Instruction Tuning
sorular.soru: A chat-format training record has a system, a user and an assistant message. What is the main job of the system message?
secenekler: It sets the overall behavior, such as how the answers should look
It holds the actual request, such as the review the model must classify
It is the target response that the model learns to produce
It chooses which weights to update and which to keep frozen
sorular.aciklama: The system message is a behavior instruction, for example which labels to use and how short the answer must be. The user message holds the request, and the assistant message is the target that the model learns to produce.

sorular.soru: A team wants a sentiment model that also explains its choice in a full sentence. Which setup can do this directly, and why?
secenekler: BERT with a classification head, because it reads the review both ways
BERT with a classification head, because the head can output any word
Either one, because both learn with cross-entropy on the label
An autoregressive LLM, because it generates the answer as text tokens
sorular.aciklama: A decoder-only LLM writes its answer token by token, so it can give a label and a reason in words. BERT with a classification head only picks one class from a fixed set, even though it reads the review in both directions.

sorular.soru: After full fine-tuning on one narrow task, a model does well on new examples of that task. But it got worse at its older skills. What explains this?
secenekler: Overfitting, because it memorized the training examples of the task
Forgetting, because updating all weights can overwrite older skills
Data leakage, because test examples got into the training data
Rounding error, because the model now stores its weights in fewer bits
sorular.aciklama: Full fine-tuning changes every weight, so it can overwrite what the model knew before. Overfitting would show as poor results on new examples of the same task, but here those results are good.

sorular.soru: Why does full fine-tuning need much more GPU memory than simply running the same model?
secenekler: It must also keep gradients and optimizer states for every weight
It must keep the whole training dataset inside the GPU at the same time
It must add new A and B matrices to every layer of the model
It must save a new full checkpoint after every training step
sorular.aciklama: Training must hold the weights plus a gradient and optimizer states for each trainable weight, and also activations for backprop. A full checkpoint is a storage cost on disk, so it does not explain the extra GPU memory.

sorular.konu: PEFT and the LoRA Mechanism (W₀, A, B)
sorular.soru: What is the main idea of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT)?
secenekler: Train a small new model from scratch, using only the task examples
Update every weight, but keep all of the optimizer states in fewer bits
Reuse the pretrained model and train only a small set of parameters
Remove the layers that the target task does not seem to need
sorular.aciklama: PEFT reuses the pretrained base and trains only a small set of selected or added parameters, which cuts gradient and optimizer costs. Training a new small model from scratch would throw away the knowledge that pretraining built.

sorular.konu: PEFT and the LoRA Mechanism (W₀, A, B)
sorular.soru: In LoRA, matrix A starts with random values and matrix B starts at zero. What is the main benefit of this starting point?
secenekler: The adapter uses less memory, because zero values take no space
Only A learns, while B stays at zero to protect the base model
The product BA starts as an exact copy of the pretrained weights
At first the adapter adds nothing, so the model starts unchanged
sorular.aciklama: With B at zero, the product BA is zero, so the adapted weight equals the frozen weight and the model first acts like the pretrained one. B does not stay at zero, because it gets the first gradient, and then both A and B learn.

sorular.konu: LoRA Hyperparameters: r, α, Dropout, Target Modules
sorular.soru: In a LoRA setup, what does the choice of target modules decide?
secenekler: How strongly the learned update acts on top of the frozen weights
Which weight matrices in the model get their own small adapter
How many trainable values each adapter matrix can hold
How often training drops parts of the adapter path at random
sorular.aciklama: Target modules are the projections, such as the query and value projections, that each get their own A and B pair. Alpha sets the strength of the update, rank sets the adapter size, and LoRA dropout does the random dropping.

sorular.konu: LoRA Hyperparameters: r, α, Dropout, Target Modules
sorular.soru: A LoRA adapter fits the training data very well but does worse on validation data. Which change is meant to help with this problem?
secenekler: Add LoRA dropout, since it regularizes the adapter in training
Raise the rank, since a bigger adapter can learn the task better
Raise alpha, since a stronger update fits the data more closely
Add more target modules, so that more layers can share the work
sorular.aciklama: LoRA dropout regularizes the adapter branch, so it is harder for the adapter to memorize the training data. A larger rank adds trainable values, and more parameters do not automatically give better results, so it can make overfitting worse.

sorular.soru: One frozen base model serves a support bot and a coding helper, each with its own LoRA adapter. What changes when the server switches between them?
secenekler: The server loads a whole new model fine-tuned for the new tool
The server trains the first adapter again on the new tool's data
Only the loaded adapter changes, and the base weights stay the same
The server raises the rank of the first adapter to cover both tools
sorular.aciklama: Each task has its own small A and B pair, while the server stores the frozen base once and shares it across all tasks. Loading a whole new model for each task is what separate full fine-tuning would need, and LoRA avoids that cost.

sorular.soru: A team already uses LoRA, but training still does not fit on their GPU. The frozen base model takes most of the memory. Which change helps most?
secenekler: Raise the rank, so that the adapters can do more of the work
Lower alpha, so that the learned update becomes much smaller
Add LoRA dropout, so that fewer adapter values stay in memory
Use QLoRA, so that the frozen base is stored in 4-bit form
sorular.aciklama: LoRA already removes most gradient and optimizer memory, but the frozen base is still large, and QLoRA shrinks it by storing it in 4-bit NF4. Lowering alpha only rescales the update and does not change how much memory the base takes.

sorular.soru: Quantization maps each weight to the nearest of a few fixed levels. Most weights sit in a narrow range. Why does NF4 put more levels in that range?
secenekler: So it can use more levels than uniform 4-bit with the same bits
So most weights land close to a level, which lowers rounding error
So the weights no longer need decoding before the multiplication
So the frozen base weights can be trained again during QLoRA
sorular.aciklama: With more levels where weights are crowded, most weights find a close level, so the average error after decoding is smaller. NF4 and uniform 4-bit have the same number of codes, and only the spacing between the levels is different.

sorular.soru: LoRA, QLoRA, AdaLoRA and DoRA each change a different part of the method. What idea do all four of them share?
secenekler: They keep the pretrained weights frozen and learn a small extra update
They store the frozen base model in 4-bit form so it uses less memory
They give each layer its own rank from one shared rank budget
They split each weight into a magnitude part and a direction part
sorular.aciklama: All four adapt a pretrained model efficiently by training a small number of added parameters while the base stays frozen. Storing the base in 4-bit is the extra step of QLoRA alone, so the other three do not share it.

sorular.soru: A team tries many LoRA ranks, picks the one with the best test score, and reports that score as the final result. What is wrong with this?
secenekler: Nothing, because the team never used the test data to update any weights
They should pick the rank on the training data, since it is the largest
The test set helped make a choice, so it is no longer a fair final check
They should add the test set to training first, and then score it again
sorular.aciklama: The team should make choices like the rank on the validation set, and use the test set once at the end to show performance on unseen data. Even without weight updates, picking the best test result tunes the setup to that test set, so the score looks better than it really is.
